blocks.html: In Earth's Spin: Day and Night you saw that Earth turns once a day, which makes the Sun rise in the east and set in the west. The same spin moves the whole night sky. Watch for a few hours and every star slides west together, the pattern never changing shape. Astronomers describe this with a simple model: the celestial sphere, a giant imaginary ball around Earth with the stars painted on the inside.

The stars are so far away that, as Earth turns, their directions stay fixed in space. We are the ones moving. Earth spins toward the east about an axis through its poles, so from the ground the whole sphere seems to turn the other way, toward the west, around two fixed points straight above Earth's poles: the north and south celestial poles. A full turn is $360^\circ$, the angles around a point (angle pairs work the same way on the sky), and it takes about 24 hours, so the sky turns $360^\circ \div 24 = 15^\circ$ every hour.

The celestial sphere is a map of directions. Because Earth spins, the sky seems to turn once a day around the celestial poles, westward at $15^\circ$ per hour. The stars are not moving across the sky; we are turning beneath them.

items: Celestial poles: the points straight above Earth's North and South Poles. Polaris, the North Star, sits less than $1^\circ$ from the north celestial pole.
Celestial equator: Earth's equator projected onto the sky, halfway between the poles.
Horizon: where the sky meets the ground for you; half the sphere is always below it.
Zenith: the point straight overhead. Meridian: the line from due north, through the zenith, to due south.

blocks.title: Star trails
blocks.q: A camera pointed at Polaris keeps its shutter open, and each star draws an arc around the pole. Every arc spans $60^\circ$. How long was the exposure?
steps: The sky turns $360^\circ$ in about 24 h, so $15^\circ$ per hour.
Every trail has the same angle because the whole sky turns as one piece, which is what a spinning Earth predicts.

blocks.html: It is natural to say the stars "move across the sky", but the stars barely change position over a lifetime. If each star moved on its own, the patterns would twist and stretch during the night. They don't: the Big Dipper keeps its shape while it circles Polaris. A quick check: in a long-exposure photo every star trail has the same angle around the pole. One thing is turning, and it is Earth.

The celestial sphere is a model, not a real shell. The stars sit at very different distances; the sphere only records their directions, which is all we need to describe how the sky turns. Try it in the Sky and Solar System lab: pick a date and a place and see which stars are up.

blocks.html: On the celestial sphere we need a way to say where a star is in your sky right now. Two angles do it. Altitude is the angle above the horizon, from $0^\circ$ on the horizon to $90^\circ$ at the zenith. Azimuth is the compass direction, measured from north toward the east: north $0^\circ$, east $90^\circ$, south $180^\circ$, west $270^\circ$.
These angles change as the sky turns and from place to place. One of them is special: the altitude of the celestial pole never changes for you, and it tells you exactly where on Earth you are.

Stand at the North Pole: the celestial pole is straight overhead, altitude $90^\circ$, and your latitude is $90^\circ$. Stand on the equator: the pole sits on the northern horizon, altitude $0^\circ$, latitude $0^\circ$. In between, every degree you walk north tilts your horizon by one degree on the curved Earth, so the pole climbs one degree. The two always match: the altitude of the north celestial pole equals your latitude. Polaris is within $1^\circ$ of the pole, so its altitude gives your latitude, which is how sailors once found theirs.
Altitude of the celestial pole = your latitude. Stars closer to the pole than that angle never set (they are circumpolar); stars that close to the opposite pole never rise.

blocks.title: Find your latitude
blocks.q: In Denver you measure Polaris $40^\circ$ above the northern horizon. What is your latitude?
steps: The pole's altitude equals the latitude, and Polaris is almost at the pole.
So the latitude is about $40^\circ$ N.

blocks.title: Which stars never set?
blocks.q: At latitude $40^\circ$ N, does a star $30^\circ$ from the north celestial pole ever set? What about one $50^\circ$ from the pole?
steps: The pole is $40^\circ$ above the northern horizon, so a circle around the pole of radius up to $40^\circ$ stays above the horizon all day.
The star $30^\circ$ from the pole circles it at a radius of $30^\circ$, dipping no lower than $40^\circ - 30^\circ = 10^\circ$ above the horizon. It never sets.
The star $50^\circ$ from the pole would dip to $40^\circ - 50^\circ = -10^\circ$: below the horizon. It rises and sets.

Astronomers give a star's angle north of the celestial equator as its declination $\delta$, so its distance from the pole is $90^\circ - \delta$. Circumpolar at $40^\circ$ N means $\delta \ge 90^\circ - 40^\circ = 50^\circ$.
blocks.a: The first never sets (circumpolar); the second rises and sets.

blocks.html: The same picture gives a star's highest altitude, when it crosses the meridian: $h_{\max} = 90^\circ - |\text{latitude} - \delta|$. A star whose declination equals your latitude passes straight overhead.

Two common mix-ups. First, Polaris is not the brightest star; it is only about the 50th brightest, and Sirius outshines it many times over. It matters because of where it is. Second, Polaris is not overhead everywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. It is overhead only at the North Pole; from Miami (latitude $26^\circ$) it hangs just $26^\circ$ up, and south of the equator it is below the horizon. Check yourself: at the equator, what is Polaris's altitude? (Zero: right on the horizon.)
In the Sky and Solar System lab you can choose your latitude and see how the stars around the pole shift.

blocks.html: Altitude and azimuth from the last lesson change every minute and from town to town. A star catalog needs coordinates that stay with the stars. The celestial sphere borrows Earth's own grid: declination is like latitude and right ascension is like longitude.

items: Declination ($\delta$): degrees north ($+$) or south ($-$) of the celestial equator, from $+90^\circ$ at the north celestial pole to $-90^\circ$ at the south one. Vega is at $+38.8^\circ$; Sirius at $-16.7^\circ$.

Right ascension (RA): how far east of a starting line a star is, measured along the celestial equator. The starting line runs through the March equinox, the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator heading north. RA is counted in hours, minutes and seconds, from $0^{\mathrm{h}}$ to $24^{\mathrm{h}}$.

blocks.html: Why hours? The sky turns $360^\circ$ in a day, so splitting the equator into 24 hours means one hour of RA turns past your meridian in one hour of time (sidereal time, see the next lesson). So $24^{\mathrm{h}} = 360^\circ$, $1^{\mathrm{h}} = 15^\circ$, and $1^{\mathrm{m}} = 15' = 0.25^\circ$. A star with RA $2^{\mathrm{h}}$ greater than another crosses your meridian 2 hours after it, every night. Because both coordinates are tied to the stars, not to you, they stay the same as the sky turns and from anywhere on Earth (they creep slowly over centuries as Earth's axis wobbles).

Declination is the sky's latitude, in degrees from the celestial equator. Right ascension is the sky's longitude, measured east from the March equinox in hours: $1^{\mathrm{h}} = 15^\circ$. A star passes overhead where your latitude equals its declination.

blocks.title: Hours to degrees
blocks.q: Sirius has right ascension $6^{\mathrm{h}}\,45^{\mathrm{m}}$. How many degrees east of the March equinox is that?
steps: $45^{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{45}{60} = 0.75$ h, so the RA is $6.75$ h.

blocks.title: Overhead where?
blocks.q: Vega has declination $+38.8^\circ$. Where on Earth does it pass straight overhead?
steps: A star reaches the zenith where the latitude equals its declination.
So at latitude $38.8^\circ$ N, near Washington, D.C., Vega passes overhead once a day.

blocks.title: Which comes first?
blocks.q: Star A has RA $5^{\mathrm{h}}\,30^{\mathrm{m}}$ and star B has RA $9^{\mathrm{h}}$. How long after A does B cross the meridian?
steps: Stars cross the meridian in order of increasing RA, because the sky turns westward.
$9 - 5.5 = 3.5$ h of RA, so B crosses about $3.5$ h after A.

blocks.html: Right ascension hours are not clock times. A star at RA $18^{\mathrm{h}}$ does not rise at 6 pm; it is $270^\circ$ east of the March equinox. The clock time it rises shifts by about 4 minutes every night, so it changes through the year while the RA stays put. Check: if RA were a clock time, the star would rise at the same time all year, but the winter and summer skies are different.

The Sun's RA does work like a clock: on the March equinox the Sun is at RA $0^{\mathrm{h}}$, and it moves about $2^{\mathrm{h}}$ east each month. See which stars are up from your own latitude in the Sky and Solar System lab.

blocks.html: A day seems simple: Earth spins once. But "once" relative to what? On the celestial sphere there are two choices, the Sun and the distant stars, and they give two different days.

items: A solar day is noon to noon, the Sun back on your meridian: $24$ h on average. Our clocks keep this day.
A sidereal day ("star day") is one turn relative to the distant stars: $23$ h $56$ min $4$ s.

blocks.html: While Earth spins, it also moves along its orbit, about $360^\circ \div 365.25 \approx 1^\circ$ per day, in the same direction as it spins. After one full $360^\circ$ turn the stars are back where they were, but the Sun now lies about $1^\circ$ farther east among them. Earth must turn that extra $1^\circ$ to bring the Sun back to the meridian. At $15^\circ$ per hour, $1^\circ$ takes about 4 minutes, so a solar day is about 4 minutes longer than a sidereal day. In rates: $\dfrac{1}{\text{sidereal day}} = \dfrac{1}{\text{solar day}} + \dfrac{1}{\text{year}}$.

A sidereal day (one spin relative to the stars) is 23 h 56 min; a solar day (noon to noon) is 24 h, because Earth also moves about $1^\circ$ along its orbit each day and must turn about $361^\circ$ to face the Sun again.

blocks.title: Stars rise earlier
blocks.q: Orion's bright star Rigel rises at 11:00 pm tonight. About when will it rise 30 days from now?
steps: Each night a star rises about 4 minutes earlier, because the clock keeps solar days and the star keeps sidereal days.
So about 9:00 pm. That is why the evening sky changes with the seasons.

blocks.title: Count the spins
blocks.q: How many times does Earth turn relative to the stars in one year?
steps: In $365.25$ solar days the Sun appears to go once around the sky relative to the stars.
That means Earth makes one more turn relative to the stars than relative to the Sun.

blocks.html: "A day is one spin of Earth" is only true for the sidereal day. From noon to noon Earth turns about $361^\circ$, not $360^\circ$. Check with the numbers: $366.25$ sidereal days of $23.934$ h make $8766$ h, the same as $365.25$ solar days of $24$ h.

Astronomers set their telescopes by sidereal time, because a star crosses the meridian at the same sidereal time every day: the sidereal time equals the right ascension on your meridian (see right ascension).

blocks.html: In Why We Have Seasons you learned that Earth's tilted axis changes how high the Sun climbs and how long it stays up. With declination we can say exactly how: the Sun's declination changes through the year, and that one number sets the solstices, the equinoxes, the tropics and the polar circles.

Earth's axis is tilted $23.4^\circ$ from the perpendicular to its orbit, and it keeps pointing the same way in space all year. So the celestial equator (above Earth's equator) is tilted $23.4^\circ$ from the ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path among the stars. As the Sun travels the ecliptic, its declination swings from $+23.4^\circ$ to $-23.4^\circ$ and back. When the North Pole leans toward the Sun (June), the Sun is $23.4^\circ$ north of the celestial equator; when it leans away (December), $23.4^\circ$ south.

blocks.html: The Sun's declination swings between $+23.4^\circ$ and $-23.4^\circ$ because of Earth's tilt. The tropics ($23.4^\circ$ N and S) are as far as the overhead Sun can go; the polar circles ($90^\circ - 23.4^\circ = 66.6^\circ$) mark where it can stay up, or down, for a whole day.

blocks.title: The midnight Sun
blocks.q: On the June solstice, poleward of what latitude does the Sun never set?
steps: On the June solstice the Sun is at declination $+23.4^\circ$, so it is $90^\circ - 23.4^\circ = 66.6^\circ$ from the north celestial pole.
From altitude and latitude: a star is circumpolar where the pole's altitude (your latitude) is at least its distance from the pole.
So the Sun stays up all day at latitude $66.6^\circ$ N and beyond: the Arctic Circle.

blocks.title: Another planet
blocks.q: Mars's axis is tilted $25.2^\circ$. Where would Mars's tropics and polar circles be?
steps: Tropics sit at the tilt: $25.2^\circ$ N and S.
Polar circles sit at $90^\circ$ minus the tilt: $90^\circ - 25.2^\circ = 64.8^\circ$.

blocks.html: The tropics and polar circles are not arbitrary lines drawn by mapmakers, and they are not where Earth is closest to the Sun. They come from the tilt alone: the tropics at the tilt angle, the polar circles at $90^\circ$ minus the tilt. A quick check: if Earth had no tilt, the Sun would stay on the celestial equator all year, the tropics would shrink to the equator, and there would be no midnight Sun anywhere except right at the poles.

Seasons do not come from Earth's distance: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in northern winter, and the distance changes only about 3%. Set dates through the year in the Sky and Solar System lab and watch Earth travel around the Sun.

blocks.html: How high does the Sun climb at noon? It depends on two numbers you already know: your latitude and the Sun's declination that day. Working with them means adding and subtracting signed numbers, as in adding and subtracting rational numbers, since south latitudes and southern declinations count as negative.

Picture the meridian, the line from the south point on the horizon through the zenith to the north. The celestial equator crosses it at an altitude of $90^\circ - \text{latitude}$ in the south (the north celestial pole is $\text{latitude}$ up in the north, and the equator is $90^\circ$ from the pole). At noon the Sun is on the meridian, $\delta$ degrees north of the celestial equator. So its altitude is $90^\circ - \text{latitude} + \delta$. In general, for any place and date, $h_{\text{noon}} = 90^\circ - |\text{latitude} - \delta|$ (count south as negative).

Noon altitude of the Sun $= 90^\circ - \text{latitude} + \delta$ for places north of the overhead Sun; in general $90^\circ - |\text{latitude} - \delta|$. With $\delta$ between $-23.4^\circ$ and $+23.4^\circ$, the Sun can be straight overhead only between the tropics.

blocks.title: Measuring Earth
blocks.q: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes knew that at noon on the June solstice the Sun was straight overhead at Syene, while at Alexandria, about 800 km north, it was $7.2^\circ$ from overhead. How big around is Earth?
steps: The Sun's rays are parallel, so the $7.2^\circ$ difference is the angle between the two cities at Earth's center.
blocks.a: About $40{,}000$ km, close to the true $40{,}075$ km.

blocks.html: Many people think the noon Sun is straight overhead everywhere, at least in summer. It never is outside the tropics. In Denver the June noon Sun reaches $73.4^\circ$; it is never at $90^\circ$, and your shadow never vanishes. Check: overhead means $h = 90^\circ$, which needs latitude $= \delta$, and $\delta$ never goes beyond $23.4^\circ$.

blocks.html: In Phases of the Moon you saw that half the Moon is always lit by the Sun, and the phase is how much of that lit half faces us. There is a second payoff to that picture: each phase has its own schedule. The Moon is not only a night object, and it does not always rise at sunset.

A phase is really an angle: how far the Moon sits east of the Sun as seen from Earth. New moon is next to the Sun ($0^\circ$); first quarter is $90^\circ$ east of it; full moon is opposite it ($180^\circ$); third quarter is $270^\circ$ east, which is $90^\circ$ west. The celestial sphere turns $15^\circ$ per hour, carrying the Sun and the Moon together. So a Moon $90^\circ$ east of the Sun rises $90 \div 15 = 6$ hours after the Sun. If the Sun rises at 6 am, the first-quarter Moon rises at noon, is highest at sunset and sets at midnight.

blocks.q: About what time does a first-quarter Moon rise, and where is it at sunset?

blocks.html: Two myths: that the Moon is only up at night, and that every phase rises at sunset. Only the full moon rises at sunset. A first-quarter Moon rises around noon and is easy to see in the afternoon sky; a third-quarter Moon is still up in the morning. Check: the Moon is up for about 12 hours of every day, so for most phases part of that time must be daylight. The Moon also rises about 50 minutes later each day, as it moves about $12^\circ$ farther east of the Sun.

blocks.html: The Moon goes around Earth in $27.3$ days relative to the stars, yet new moon to new moon takes $29.5$ days. If that sounds familiar, it should: it is the same puzzle as the solar and sidereal days, on a bigger scale. And since phases depend on the Sun, as in moon phases and moonrise times, the phase cycle uses the Sun as its reference.

items: Sidereal month: one orbit relative to the stars, $27.32$ days.
Synodic month: one cycle of phases, new moon to new moon, $29.53$ days.

blocks.html: In $27.3$ days Earth carries the Earth–Moon pair about $27^\circ$ along its orbit, so the Sun appears about $27^\circ$ farther east among the stars. When the Moon is back at the same stars, it still has to catch up those $27^\circ$ to be lined up with the Sun again, which takes about two more days. In rates: the Moon moves $360^\circ / 27.32 = 13.18^\circ$ per day against the stars, the Sun $360^\circ / 365.25 = 0.99^\circ$ per day, so the Moon gains $12.19^\circ$ per day on the Sun and needs $360^\circ / 12.19^\circ = 29.53$ days to lap it. As a formula: $\dfrac{1}{S} = \dfrac{1}{P} - \dfrac{1}{Y}$.

Synodic month $S$ (phases): $\dfrac{1}{S} = \dfrac{1}{P_{\text{sidereal}}} - \dfrac{1}{P_{\text{year}}}$, giving $29.53$ days, longer than the $27.32$-day orbit because Earth moves along its orbit too.

blocks.title: A planet's cycle
blocks.q: Mars orbits the Sun in $1.88$ years. How often does Earth pass Mars (from one opposition to the next)?
steps: Earth laps Mars, so use the faster minus the slower rate: $\frac{1}{S} = \frac{1}{1} - \frac{1}{1.88} = 1 - 0.532 = 0.468$ per year.
That is how often Mars is closest and brightest, and how often it loops backward in our sky.

blocks.html: Time it yourself in the Sky and Solar System lab: run the Moon through a few months and count the days from one new moon to the next.

It is easy to think the phases repeat once per orbit. They repeat once per lap of the Sun, which takes longer. Check with the numbers: after $27.3$ days the Moon is back among the same stars, but it is a crescent, not new. The extra $2.2$ days is the time to catch up with the Sun's $27^\circ$ move.

blocks.html: From Solar and Lunar Eclipses you know an eclipse needs the Sun, Earth and Moon in a line: a solar eclipse at new moon, when the Moon's shadow falls on Earth, and a lunar eclipse at full moon, when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow. New and full moons come every month, so why are eclipses rare?

The Moon's orbit is tilted about $5^\circ$ to the plane of Earth's orbit. The two planes cross along a line, the line of nodes. Most months, the new moon passes up to $5^\circ$ above or below the Sun, which is about ten times the Sun's width of $0.53^\circ$, and the shadow misses Earth. An eclipse needs a new or full moon close to a node. The tilted orbit keeps its direction in space as Earth circles the Sun, so twice a year the line of nodes points at the Sun. Those windows, each about five weeks long, are the eclipse seasons.

Because the Moon's orbit is tilted about $5^\circ$, eclipses happen only when a new or full moon falls near a node, during eclipse seasons about 173 days apart. Every year has at least two solar eclipses somewhere on Earth.

blocks.title: How far apart?
blocks.q: The line of nodes points at the Sun once per half of an eclipse year of $346.6$ days. How far apart are the eclipse seasons?
steps: $346.6 \div 2 = 173.3$ days: a little under six months.
The eclipse year is shorter than the calendar year because the nodes slide slowly westward, so the seasons arrive about 19 days earlier each year.

blocks.title: Total or annular?
blocks.q: The Moon is $3474$ km across. During one solar eclipse it is $400{,}000$ km away. The Sun looks $0.533^\circ$ wide. Total or annular?
steps: Small-angle rule: angle $\approx 57.3^\circ \times \frac{\text{diameter}}{\text{distance}}$ ($57.3^\circ$ is one radian).

That is smaller than the Sun, so a bright ring stays visible: an annular eclipse. Near its closest, about $357{,}000$ km, the Moon looks $0.558^\circ$ wide and can cover the Sun completely: a total eclipse.

blocks.html: "There should be an eclipse every month" is a natural guess if you picture the Moon's orbit flat. It is tilted, so most new moons pass above or below the Sun and most full moons pass above or below Earth's shadow. Check with numbers: $5.1^\circ \div 0.53^\circ \approx 10$, so the new moon can miss the Sun by about ten Sun-widths.

A solar eclipse is seen only along the narrow path of the Moon's shadow, while a lunar eclipse is seen from the whole night side of Earth, which is why most people have seen more lunar eclipses. Find the eclipse seasons yourself in the Sky and Solar System lab.

blocks.html: On the celestial sphere the stars keep their places, but five bright "wanderers" (the Greek word is planetes) drift slowly among them: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Usually they creep eastward from night to night. Every so often one stops, moves backward (westward) for weeks, stops again and resumes its eastward path. This retrograde motion was the great puzzle of ancient astronomy.

Ptolemy's Earth-centered model (about AD 150) explained the loops with circles on circles, called epicycles. In 1543 Copernicus proposed something simpler: the Sun is at the center, Earth is one planet among the others, and the loops are an effect of our own motion.

In a Sun-centered system every planet always moves forward around the Sun, and the inner ones move faster. Earth, on the inside track, regularly catches up with Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. While we pass, our line of sight to the outer planet swings backward against the distant stars, just as a slower car seems to drift backward against far-off hills when you pass it on the highway. Nothing actually reverses. And the loops come exactly when Earth passes the planet, when it is opposite the Sun in our sky and at its brightest, which is what the model predicts.

In the Sun-centered (heliocentric) model, retrograde loops are an illusion caused by Earth overtaking a slower outer planet (or a faster inner planet overtaking us). Galileo's observation that Venus shows a full set of phases, large as a crescent and small when nearly full, settled the case against Ptolemy's model.

blocks.html: In 1610 Galileo turned a telescope on Venus. In Ptolemy's model Venus always stays between Earth and the Sun, so it could only ever show crescent phases. Galileo saw it go through all the phases, from a big thin crescent to a small, nearly full disk. A nearly full Venus has to be on the far side of the Sun from us, which only a Sun-centered orbit allows. He also found four moons circling Jupiter, proof that not everything goes around Earth.

blocks.title: Venus near and far
blocks.q: Venus orbits the Sun at $0.72$ AU and Earth at $1$ AU. How many times larger does Venus look at its closest than at its farthest?
steps: Closest, between us and the Sun: $1 - 0.72 = 0.28$ AU. Farthest, beyond the Sun: $1 + 0.72 = 1.72$ AU.
Apparent size is inversely proportional to distance: $\frac{1.72}{0.28} \approx 6.1$.
The crescent phase comes when Venus is close, and the full phase when it is far: big crescents and small full disks, as Galileo saw.

blocks.html: A retrograde planet does not really loop backward in space, any more than a car you pass on the highway really drives backward. Check: if the loops were real motion, they would happen at random places in the orbit. Instead each one comes exactly when Earth passes the planet, when it is opposite the Sun and brightest.

blocks.html: Copernicus kept one old idea from the Earth-centered model: orbits had to be perfect circles. His predictions were better than Ptolemy's, but Mars still drifted away from them. Johannes Kepler spent years fitting Tycho Brahe's careful measurements of Mars and in 1609 found the answer: the orbit is not a circle but an ellipse.

items: An ellipse is a stretched circle. It has two special points inside it, the foci. For every point on the ellipse, the distances to the two foci add up to the same total, $2a$.
The semi-major axis $a$ is half the long axis; it is the planet's average distance from the Sun.
The eccentricity $e = c/a$, where $c$ is the distance from the center to a focus. $e = 0$ is a circle; $e$ close to $1$ is long and thin.

blocks.html: Kepler's first law: each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; the other focus is empty. Since the Sun sits a distance $c = ae$ from the center, the closest point (perihelion) is $a - ae = a(1 - e)$ from the Sun and the farthest point (aphelion) is $a + ae = a(1 + e)$. Adding them gives $2a$; subtracting gives $2ae$. Newton later showed that an inverse-square force like gravity produces exactly these ellipses.
Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. Perihelion $= a(1 - e)$, aphelion $= a(1 + e)$, and $a$ is their average. For the planets, $e$ is small: their ellipses are nearly circles.

blocks.html: Textbook drawings stretch planetary orbits so the ellipse is easy to see, and many people come away thinking orbits are long, thin ovals. Real planetary orbits are nearly circles: Earth's $e = 0.017$ means the Sun is only $1.7\%$ of the way from the center to the edge. Long, thin orbits belong to comets. blocks.html: Kepler's first law gives the shape of an orbit. His second law tells how a planet moves along it, and the answer surprised him: not at a steady speed.

Imagine a line from the Sun to the planet. Kepler found that this line sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the line is short, so to sweep a given area in a month the planet must cover a long stretch of its path: it moves fast. Far from the Sun the line is long, and a short stretch of path sweeps the same area: it moves slowly. Newton explained why. Gravity pulls straight toward the Sun, never sideways, so it never speeds up or slows down the planet's turning around the Sun (its angular momentum stays fixed). At perihelion and aphelion, where the motion is straight across the line to the Sun, this means $v_p\, r_p = v_a\, r_a$.
A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion: $v_p\, r_p = v_a\, r_a$.

blocks.title: Earth's two speeds
blocks.q: Earth is $147.1$ million km from the Sun at perihelion (early January) and $152.1$ million km at aphelion (early July). How much faster does it move in January?
steps: At the ends of the orbit: $\frac{v_p}{v_a} = \frac{r_a}{r_p}$.
Earth moves about $3.4\%$ faster in January, which is one reason northern winter is a few days shorter than northern summer.

steps: $v_a = 4$ km/s: ten times farther, ten times slower.

blocks.html: It is natural to picture a planet cruising at one steady speed, but along an ellipse its speed changes all the time. Check with Earth: the March equinox to the September equinox (northern spring and summer, Earth farther out and slower) lasts about 186 days, while the other half of the year lasts about 179.

blocks.html: Kepler's second law covers one planet. In 1619 he found a rule that links them all: the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year, in a precise way. It uses the fractional exponents you know: $P = a^{3/2}$.

Measure the period $P$ in years and the semi-major axis $a$ in AU, and for every planet $P^2 = a^3$. Two things stretch an outer planet's year. Its path is longer, in proportion to $a$. And gravity is weaker out there, so it moves more slowly: for circular orbits, speed goes as $1/\sqrt{a}$. Time is path divided by speed: $P \propto a \div \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} = a^{3/2}$, so $P^2 \propto a^3$. Earth sets the units: $1$ AU and $1$ year make the constant $1$.
Kepler's third law: $P^2 = a^3$ ($P$ in years, $a$ in AU, for bodies orbiting the Sun). So $P = a^{3/2}$ and $a = P^{2/3}$. Twice as far means $2^{3/2} \approx 2.8$ times as long.

blocks.html: Kepler's third law was a pattern; Newton explained it, and in doing so turned every orbit into a scale for weighing the body at the center. You know from Gravity: Mass and Distance that more mass means more pull. More pull means a faster orbit.

Take a small body on a circular orbit of radius $a$ around a mass $M$. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\frac{GMm}{a^2} = \frac{mv^2}{a}$, so $v^2 = \frac{GM}{a}$. The small mass $m$ cancels. One orbit takes $P = \frac{2\pi a}{v}$, so $v = \frac{2\pi a}{P}$. Substituting: $\frac{4\pi^2 a^2}{P^2} = \frac{GM}{a}$, which gives $$M = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G P^2}.$$ The same result holds for ellipses with $a$ the semi-major axis. In the Sun's units (AU, years, solar masses), Earth's orbit makes every constant equal to 1, leaving $M = \frac{a^3}{P^2}$. (Strictly, $M$ is the sum of both masses; a planet adds almost nothing.)

Newton's form of Kepler's third law: $M = \dfrac{a^3}{P^2}$ with $M$ in solar masses, $a$ in AU and $P$ in years; in SI units, $M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G P^2}$. The orbit measures the mass at the center.

blocks.html: It seems natural that a heavier satellite would orbit faster or slower, but the orbiting body's own mass cancels out of $\frac{GMm}{a^2} = \frac{mv^2}{a}$. A space station and a dropped bolt beside it orbit together. That is why an orbit weighs the central body. Check: the Moon (about $1\%$ of Earth's mass) and a tiny satellite at the Moon's distance would have almost exactly the same 27-day period.
This is how astronomers know the masses of the Sun, the planets with moons, distant stars with planets, and the black hole at the center of our galaxy.

blocks.html: In Gravity and Orbits you met the idea that an orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground. With Newton's law of gravity we can find exactly how fast "fast enough" is, and how fast you must go to leave for good.

Newton imagined a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire a ball sideways and it falls to the ground. Fire faster and it lands farther away. At one special speed the ground curves away under the ball exactly as fast as the ball falls: it keeps falling and never lands. That is a circular orbit, where gravity provides the centripetal force: $\frac{GM}{r^2} = \frac{v^2}{r}$, so $v_c = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$. To escape, the kinetic energy must at least cancel the gravitational potential energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{r}$, so $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}} = \sqrt{2}\,v_c$.

Circular orbital speed $v_c = \sqrt{GM/r}$, with $r$ measured from the planet's center. Escape speed $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r} = \sqrt{2}\,v_c$. At Earth's surface: about $7.9$ km/s to orbit and $11.2$ km/s to escape.

blocks.q: A spacecraft in a low circular orbit around the Moon moves at $1.68$ km/s. What speed would it need to escape from there?
steps: $v_{\text{esc}} = 2.38$ km/s, far less than Earth's $11.2$ km/s.

blocks.html: A spacecraft does not need to keep firing its engines to stay in orbit. Gravity at $400$ km is still about $90\%$ as strong as on the ground; the astronauts float because they and the station fall together. Moving sideways at $7.7$ km/s, the station needs no push to keep going (Newton's first law); it fires its thrusters only now and then to make up for the drag of the thin air. Check: the Moon has orbited Earth for billions of years with no engine at all.
Higher orbits are slower: geostationary satellites, $35{,}786$ km up, move at only $3.07$ km/s. Try launching from the mountain yourself in the Orbit Lab.

blocks.html: In Tides you saw how the Moon raises two bulges of ocean, giving most coasts two high tides a day. The Sun raises tides too. Whether its tides add to the Moon's or work against them depends on the phase of the Moon.

Tides come from the difference in gravity across Earth (see how gravity depends on distance). The side of Earth facing the Moon is pulled a little more than Earth's center, and the far side a little less, so Earth is stretched along the Earth–Moon line. That difference falls off as $M/d^3$, faster than gravity itself. The Sun is 27 million times more massive than the Moon but 390 times farther away: $2.7 \times 10^7 \div 390^3 \approx 0.46$. So the Sun's tides are a little under half as strong as the Moon's. When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up (new and full moon) the two pairs of bulges line up and add. At the quarter moons, the Sun's bulges sit at right angles to the Moon's and partly cancel them.

Spring tides (the largest range) come at new and full moon, when the Sun's and Moon's tides add. Neap tides (the smallest range) come at first and third quarter, when they partly cancel. Each comes about every two weeks, all year round.

blocks.html: The word "spring" in spring tide has nothing to do with the season. It comes from the water springing up. Spring tides happen twice every month, in January as much as in April. Check: new moon happens about every 29.5 days, all year, and each one brings a spring tide.

blocks.html: In Light-Years, Stars and Galaxies you met the light-year as a distance. Here is the other side of that idea: because light needs time to reach us, every look into space is a look into the past. Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, and all of it, from radio to gamma rays, travels through space at the same speed, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{5}$ km/s.

Light is fast but not instant. In 1676 Ole Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io came several minutes late when Jupiter was far from Earth and early when it was near: the light carrying the news needed extra time to cross the wider gap. Travel time is distance divided by speed, $t = \dfrac{d}{c}$. A light-year is how far light goes in one year: $3.00 \times 10^{5}\ \text{km/s} \times 3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s} = 9.46 \times 10^{12}$ km. So light from an object $N$ light-years away left it $N$ years ago. The numbers are huge, so operations in scientific notation do most of the work.

Light takes time $t = d/c$ to reach us, so we see every object as it was when its light left: the Sun as it was $8.3$ minutes ago, the nearest star $4.2$ years ago, the Andromeda Galaxy about $2.5$ million years ago.

blocks.html: It is natural to think we see the stars as they are now. We never do. The light from Betelgeuse left it centuries ago; if it exploded tonight, nobody on Earth would know for hundreds of years. Check the units: a light-year is a distance, and the travel time in years equals the distance in light-years. The farther away we look, the older the view, which is how astronomers study the young universe: they look very far.

blocks.html: Look closely at the night sky and the stars are not all white: Betelgeuse is orange-red, Rigel blue-white, the Sun yellow-white. Those colors are thermometers. A hot, dense object (a star, a stove coil, you) gives off a smooth rainbow of light called thermal or blackbody radiation, spread across the electromagnetic spectrum, and its shape depends only on temperature.

In a hot object, atoms and electrons jostle with energies set by the temperature, and the light they give off carries those energies. Hotter means more energetic jostling, so more energetic photons, which have shorter wavelengths. The curve of brightness against wavelength has one peak, and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths in exact proportion as the object heats up. This is Wien's law: $$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{6}\ \text{nm·K}}{T}.$$ The temperature must be in kelvins, counted from absolute zero (see temperature scales).
Wien's law: $\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \dfrac{2.90 \times 10^{6}\ \text{nm·K}}{T}$. Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths, so blue-white stars are the hottest and red stars the coolest.

blocks.html: Everyday language calls red "hot" and blue "cold", but for glowing objects it is the other way around. A stove coil glows dull red at about $1000$ K; a welding arc glows blue-white at several thousand kelvins. Check with Wien's law: a shorter peak wavelength (blue) needs a larger $T$.

blocks.html: A star's luminosity $L$ is its total power: the energy it sends out each second, in watts. The Sun's is $3.83 \times 10^{26}$ W. From Wien's law you know temperature sets a star's color. Temperature also sets how much power each square meter of its surface gives off, and the size of the surface does the rest.

Each square meter of a hot surface radiates $\sigma T^4$ watts (the Stefan–Boltzmann law, with $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W/(m}^2\text{K}^4)$). The fourth power is steep: double the temperature and each square meter gives off $2^4 = 16$ times as much. A star's surface is a sphere of area $4\pi R^2$. So $$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4.$$ Divide by the Sun's values and every constant cancels: in solar units (radius in $R_\odot$, temperature in units of the Sun's $5772$ K), $L = R^2 T^4$. The exponent rules make this quick: $(2R)^2 = 4R^2$ and $(2T)^4 = 16T^4$.

$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$; in solar units, $L = R^2 T^4$. Luminosity depends on size and temperature together, so a cool star can be very luminous if it is huge, and a hot star can be faint if it is tiny.

blocks.html: In Bright-Line Spectra you saw that each element gives off its own set of colors, because its electrons can only drop between certain energy levels. Astronomers use those fingerprints to read what stars, nebulae and galaxies are made of, across trillions of kilometers. The key is that there are three kinds of spectra, and each comes from a different situation.

items: Continuous spectrum: a hot, dense object (a solid, a liquid, or a dense gas like a star's interior) gives off every wavelength, a smooth rainbow.
Emission (bright-line) spectrum: a hot, thin gas gives off light only at its own wavelengths.
Absorption (dark-line) spectrum: a cooler, thin gas in front of a hotter continuous source removes light at those same wavelengths, leaving dark lines.

blocks.html: These are Kirchhoff's laws, and energy levels explain them. An electron dropping from a higher level to a lower one emits a photon with exactly the energy difference, $E = hc/\lambda$. Going the other way, an electron can absorb a photon only if it has exactly the energy to lift it between two levels. Same levels, same energies, same wavelengths: a gas absorbs precisely the wavelengths it would emit. In a star, the hot, dense interior makes the continuous light, and the cooler gas in its outer layers absorbs its own wavelengths, so starlight shows dark lines.
Hot and dense: continuous. Hot, thin gas: bright lines. Cool gas in front of a hotter source: dark lines at the very same wavelengths. Either way, the lines identify the element.

blocks.q: Hydrogen's red line is at $656.3$ nm. What energy does each of its photons carry? Use $hc = 1240$ eV·nm.
steps: That matches the gap between hydrogen's levels 3 and 2: $-1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89$ eV.

blocks.title: Read the spectrum
blocks.q: Light from a star passes through a cool cloud of sodium gas before reaching us. What do we see near $589$ nm?
steps: The star gives a continuous spectrum.
The cooler sodium in front absorbs its own wavelengths, $589.0$ and $589.6$ nm.
So we see a rainbow with two dark lines there: an absorption spectrum.

blocks.html: A natural guess is that dark lines mean the star lacks that element. It is the opposite: dark lines at sodium's wavelengths show that sodium atoms are there, in the cooler gas between us and the hot layers below, absorbing those colors. Check: the same element's bright lines in the lab fall at exactly the same wavelengths as its dark lines in the star. Helium was discovered this way, in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, before anyone found it on Earth.

blocks.html: A siren sounds higher as it comes toward you and lower as it goes away: the Doppler effect. Light does the same. With spectral lines as precise markers, astronomers can measure how fast any star or galaxy is moving toward or away from us, from its light alone.

A source moving away from us emits each wave crest from a little farther away than the last, so the crests arrive stretched apart: longer wavelengths, a redshift. A source moving toward us squeezes the crests together: a blueshift. In one wave period $T$ the source moves $vT$, so the wavelength changes by $\Delta\lambda = vT$ while the wavelength itself is $\lambda = cT$. Dividing, $$\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{c}.$$ This holds for speeds much less than $c$, and it measures only the radial velocity, the motion along our line of sight; sideways motion does not shift the lines.
$\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{v}{c}$. Lines shifted to longer wavelengths (redshift) mean the source is moving away; shorter (blueshift) means toward us.

blocks.html: You know from Refraction and Lenses that a lens bends light to a focus. A telescope uses a big lens (a refractor) or a curved mirror (a reflector) to bring light from a distant object to a focus, where an eye, a camera or a spectrograph collects it. Every large research telescope today is a reflector, because a mirror can be supported from behind and has no color fringes.

Most things in the sky are faint, so a telescope's first job is to gather light. It catches every photon that lands on its mirror, so the light gathered is proportional to the area, $\pi D^2/4$: double the diameter, four times the light. Its second job is to resolve detail. Light spreading as waves (diffraction) blurs every point into a tiny disk, of angular size about $1.22\lambda/D$ radians; in arcseconds, $\theta \approx 2.5 \times 10^{5}\,\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$. A wider aperture makes a smaller blur. Magnification, $f_{\text{objective}}/f_{\text{eyepiece}}$, comes third: it only spreads out whatever light and detail the aperture captured.

Light-gathering power grows as $D^2$; the finest resolvable angle is about $2.5 \times 10^{5}\,\lambda/D$ arcseconds. Both depend on the aperture $D$, which is why astronomers build ever larger mirrors.

Stars are so far away that even the biggest telescope shows them as points; what it shows is more of them, fainter ones, and finer detail in extended objects. Extra magnification without more aperture only makes a bigger, dimmer blur. Check: telescopes are named by their diameter (a "10 m telescope"), never by their magnification.

blocks.html: Visible light is a thin slice of the electromagnetic spectrum. Cold gas clouds glow in radio waves, dust-wrapped newborn stars in infrared, and the hottest gas around black holes in X-rays. To see the whole universe, astronomers build telescopes for every band, and where they put them depends on what our air lets through.

Earth's atmosphere absorbs most wavelengths. The thin upper air soaks up gamma rays and X-rays, and the ozone layer stops most ultraviolet (which is good for living things). Water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb much of the infrared. Only two broad "windows" stay open: visible light (with a little near infrared and ultraviolet around it) and radio waves from about a centimeter to around ten meters. So optical and radio telescopes can sit on the ground, while X-ray, gamma-ray, most ultraviolet and far-infrared telescopes must fly above the atmosphere. Infrared telescopes also need to be cold, or their own warmth glows in the very light they are trying to see.

The atmosphere is open to visible light and radio waves, so those telescopes work from the ground. Gamma-ray, X-ray, most ultraviolet and far-infrared telescopes must go to space (some infrared work is possible from high, dry mountains).

blocks.html: In Planets, Moons and Small Bodies you sorted the planets into small rocky ones near the Sun and giants farther out. One number tells the two families apart and reveals what each planet is made of, even ones no spacecraft has landed on: its average density.

Density is mass divided by volume, $\rho = \frac{M}{V}$. We can measure both from far away. A planet's mass comes from the orbits of its moons or of passing spacecraft (see weighing with orbits), and its radius from its angular size and distance. A planet is close to a sphere, so $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (volume of spheres). Then we compare with known materials: water is $1$ g/cm³, rock about $3$, iron about $8$, and hydrogen and helium far less. A planet's average density tells the mix.

Average density $= \dfrac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}$. Rocky (terrestrial) planets come out at about $4$ to $5.5$ g/cm³: rock with iron cores. The giants come out at about $0.7$ to $1.6$ g/cm³: mostly hydrogen and helium (Jupiter, Saturn) or ices (Uranus, Neptune) around small dense cores.

The opposite is true: Jupiter is 318 times Earth's mass but about 1300 times its volume, so it is only a quarter as dense. Density compares mass with volume; size alone tells nothing. Earth's density is a little higher than it would be uncompressed, because its own weight squeezes the deep rock and iron. The Moon, at $3.34$ g/cm³, has only a small iron core.

blocks.html: The two families of planets are not an accident. They are fossils of how the solar system formed, about 4.6 billion years ago, from a cloud of gas and dust. Astronomers have since watched the same process happening around young stars.

A cloud of gas and dust, slowly turning, begins to collapse under its own gravity. As it shrinks it spins faster, because its angular momentum (which goes as $r^2\omega$ for each spinning part) stays the same, like a skater pulling in her arms. Spinning fast, it cannot collapse along its equator as easily as along its axis, so it flattens into a disk. Most of the mass falls to the center and becomes the Sun. In the disk, grains of dust stick together into pebbles, then into kilometer-sized planetesimals, which collide and grow into planets. What could freeze depended on temperature: near the young Sun only rock and metal could condense, but beyond the frost line, a few AU out, ices froze too. With much more solid material out there, large cores formed quickly and pulled in hydrogen and helium gas: the giants.

The solar nebula collapsed and spun up into a flat disk; the Sun formed at the center and the planets formed beside it, in the disk. Rock and metal condensed everywhere, ices only beyond the frost line, which is why small rocky planets lie inside and giants outside.

blocks.html: An old idea is that the planets formed from material torn or thrown out of the Sun. The evidence points the other way: the planets formed in the disk around the Sun, at the same time as the Sun. Check: material from the Sun would be mostly hydrogen and helium everywhere, yet the inner planets are rock and metal, sorted by temperature just as the disk model predicts.

blocks.html: The planet-building process left leftovers: rocky and metallic asteroids, most between Mars and Jupiter (about $2.1$ to $3.3$ AU), and icy comets, which spend most of their time far out, in the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune or the much more distant Oort cloud.

A comet's nucleus is a lump of ice and dust a few kilometers across. Far from the Sun it is frozen and dark. On a long, stretched orbit it falls in toward the Sun, where sunlight warms it: ices turn to gas, releasing dust, and a huge glowing cloud, the coma, surrounds it. Two forces then shape the tails. The solar wind, a stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun, sweeps the gas straight away from the Sun in a bluish ion tail. Sunlight itself gently pushes the dust away, into a broader, curved dust tail. Both pushes point away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is going.

Comets are icy leftovers on long, stretched orbits. Near the Sun they grow comas and tails that always point away from the Sun. When Earth passes through dust a comet has left along its orbit, the grains burn up in our air as a meteor shower, on the same dates each year.

blocks.html: A meteoroid is a small bit of rock or dust in space; when one plunges into the atmosphere at tens of kilometers per second and glows, it is a meteor; a piece that survives to the ground is a meteorite. Comets shed dust all along their orbits. Earth crosses some of these trails at the same point in its orbit each year, so showers return on schedule: the Perseids every August from Comet Swift–Tuttle, the Orionids every October from Halley's Comet.

blocks.html: For centuries, planets around other stars were a guess. The first one around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was found in 1995, and today more than 5,000 are confirmed (NASA Exoplanet Archive). Hardly any were seen directly: a planet is billions of times fainter than its star and lost in its glare. Instead astronomers watch the star, using ideas you already know: Doppler shifts and orbits.

Transits. If a planet's orbit is edge-on to us, the planet crosses its star's face once per orbit and blocks a small disk of light. The fraction blocked is the ratio of the two disks' areas: $\dfrac{\pi R_p^2}{\pi R_\star^2} = \left(\dfrac{R_p}{R_\star}\right)^2$. The depth gives the planet's size; the time between dips gives its period. Wobble. A star and its planet both orbit their common center of mass, so the star moves in a small circle, and its spectral lines shift back and forth. Balancing momenta, $M_\star v_\star = m_p v_p$, so the size of the wobble gives the planet's mass.

Transit depth $= \left(\dfrac{R_p}{R_\star}\right)^2$ gives a planet's size; the star's Doppler wobble, $v_\star = v_p\,\dfrac{m_p}{M_\star}$, gives its mass. Together they give its density: rocky or gassy.

blocks.html: Energy always flows from hot to cold, outward from the 15-million-kelvin core. Deep inside, the gas is so dense that light travels only a tiny distance before being absorbed and sent off in a random direction, so energy drifts outward through the radiative zone over tens of thousands of years or more. Farther out, the gas is cool enough that light gets trapped more easily, and it becomes faster to move energy by carrying hot gas upward: convection. At the photosphere the gas is thin enough for light to fly straight out. The Sun is hot plasma all the way through; the photosphere is just the depth we can see down to.

Core (fusion), radiative zone (energy carried by light), convective zone (energy carried by moving gas), photosphere (the visible surface), chromosphere and corona (the atmosphere). The Sun is gas all the way down, with no solid surface.

There is no solid surface: the Sun is gas (plasma) from the corona to the center. The edge looks sharp only because the photosphere, where the gas turns from opaque to clear, is just a few hundred kilometers thick, tiny next to the Sun's radius. Check: a spacecraft falling in would never land on anything; it would just meet hotter, denser gas.

blocks.html: The Sun's core is the power plant. You met fusion in Fission and Fusion: light nuclei joining into heavier ones, with a little mass disappearing as energy. In the Sun the fuel is hydrogen and the product is helium.

Four hydrogen nuclei (protons) end up as one helium-4 nucleus, through a series of steps called the proton–proton chain (along the way two protons turn into neutrons, giving off positrons and neutrinos). Weigh both sides with atomic masses: $4 \times 1.007825 = 4.031300$ u before, $4.002603$ u after. The difference, $0.028697$ u, is $0.71\%$ of the starting mass, and it leaves as energy, $E = mc^2$: $0.028697 \times 931.5 = 26.7$ MeV per helium nucleus. Protons repel each other, so fusion needs extreme heat and pressure: about 15 million K and enormous density in the core, where nuclei collide fast enough, with help from quantum tunneling, to fuse.

The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium in its core; about $0.7\%$ of the mass becomes energy by $E = mc^2$. To give off $3.83 \times 10^{26}$ W it turns about $4.3 \times 10^{9}$ kg of mass into energy every second.

steps: Burning $1$ kg of coal gives about $3 \times 10^{7}$ J: fusion gives about 20 million times as much.

blocks.q: The Sun gives off $3.83 \times 10^{26}$ W. How much mass does it turn into energy each second, and how much hydrogen does it fuse?
steps: Mass per second $= \frac{L}{c^2} = \frac{3.83 \times 10^{26}}{9.00 \times 10^{16}} = 4.26 \times 10^{9}$ kg/s, over 4 million tonnes a second.
That is $0.7\%$ of the hydrogen fused: $\frac{4.26 \times 10^{9}}{0.007} = 6.1 \times 10^{11}$ kg/s, about 600 million tonnes every second.
Even at that rate, the Sun's $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg lasts billions of years.
blocks.a: $4.26 \times 10^{9}$ kg/s converted; $6.1 \times 10^{11}$ kg/s of hydrogen fused.

blocks.html: The Sun is not burning like a fire. Burning is a chemical reaction that needs oxygen and releases only about $10^{7}$ J per kilogram; a Sun made of coal would burn out in a few thousand years. Check: Earth's rocks are billions of years old, and only nuclear fusion, millions of times richer than burning, can keep the Sun shining that long.

blocks.html: A car's range is the fuel in its tank divided by how fast it burns fuel. The Sun is the same. With fusion as the fuel and its luminosity as the burn rate, scientific notation turns a big question into a short calculation: how long can the Sun shine?

Lifetime $=$ energy available $\div$ power. Only the core gets hot enough to fuse, and by the time the core has turned about a tenth of the Sun's hydrogen into helium, the Sun begins to change. So the energy available is about $0.1 \times 0.007 \times M_\odot c^2$. Divide by $L_\odot$, and the answer is about 10 billion years. Alternatives fail this test badly: a Sun that burned chemically would last a few thousand years, and one that shone only by slowly shrinking (gravity heating it) would last about 30 million years. Rocks and meteorites show the solar system is 4.6 billion years old, so only fusion fits.

Main-sequence lifetime $\approx \dfrac{\text{fuel}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{0.1 \times 0.007\,M_\odot c^2}{L_\odot} \approx 10$ billion years for the Sun. It is about 4.6 billion years old, so about halfway through.

blocks.html: Two opposite myths: that the Sun will burn out within a few thousand years, and that it will end in a supernova. It has about 5 billion years of hydrogen left in its core. And it is far too light to explode: only stars of more than about 8 solar masses end as supernovae. The Sun will swell into a red giant, puff off its outer layers, and leave a white dwarf. Check: a supernova needs a heavy iron core collapsing, and the Sun will never make iron.

blocks.html: The photosphere is not smooth and steady. Dark sunspots come and go, and their number rises and falls in a cycle of about 11 years. The cause is magnetism. You know from Magnets and Magnetic Fields that magnets have field lines running from north to south poles. The Sun is a giant, churning magnet.

The Sun's gas is a plasma, full of charged particles, so it drags magnetic field lines along as it moves. The Sun also spins faster at its equator (about 25 days) than near its poles (about 35), and its convective zone boils. Together these wind up and twist the field until bundles of it burst through the surface in loops. Where a strong loop comes out, its field pushes back on the hot gas rising from below and slows the flow of heat. That patch cools to about $3800$ to $4500$ K, against about $5800$ K around it, and so it looks dark. Every 11 years or so the tangled field reorganizes, and the Sun's magnetic poles flip; the full magnetic cycle takes about 22 years.
Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where strong magnetic fields block the heat coming up from below. Their number rises and falls about every 11 years, along with flares and other solar activity.

blocks.title: How dark is a sunspot?
blocks.q: A sunspot is at $4000$ K and the photosphere around it at $5800$ K. Power per square meter goes as $T^4$. How bright is the spot compared with its surroundings?
steps: The spot gives off about a quarter as much light per square meter, so it looks dark by contrast, though on its own it would still glow brighter than the filament of a light bulb.

blocks.title: Watching the Sun turn
blocks.q: A sunspot near the equator takes about $27$ days to go once around as seen from Earth. How long does it take to cross the visible half of the disk?
steps: The visible half is half a turn: $27 \div 2 = 13.5$ days.
Galileo used sunspots this way to show that the Sun rotates.

blocks.html: Sunspots are neither holes in the Sun nor hotter spots. They are cooler, by well over a thousand kelvins, which is why they look dark next to the brighter gas around them. Check with $T^4$: a $4000$ K patch beside a $5800$ K surface gives off only about a quarter as much light per square meter.

Above active regions, twisted fields can snap and reconnect, releasing flares and huge clouds of plasma (coronal mass ejections). When these reach Earth they cause auroras and can disturb satellites and power grids. NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center tracks them.

blocks.html: Hold a finger up at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps against the background. Bring it closer and it jumps more. That shift is parallax, and it is the one direct way to measure the distance to a star: no assumptions about the star, just geometry. The baseline is Earth's own orbit, measured in AU, the unit from Kepler's third law.

Photograph a nearby star in January, then again in July, from the other side of Earth's orbit, $2$ AU away. Against much more distant stars, the nearby one seems to shift. Half of that shift is the parallax angle $p$: the angle the $1$ AU radius of Earth's orbit spans as seen from the star. For such tiny angles, angle $\approx \frac{\text{size}}{\text{distance}}$ (in radians), so the distance is $d = \frac{1\ \text{AU}}{p}$. Astronomers made this neat by defining a unit to match: one parsec (parallax-second) is the distance at which $1$ AU spans $1$ arcsecond ($\frac{1}{3600}$ of a degree, about the angle a quarter makes seen from $5$ km away). With $p$ in arcseconds, $d = \frac{1}{p}$ parsecs. Since $1$ arcsecond is $\frac{1}{206{,}265}$ radian, $1$ pc $= 206{,}265$ AU $= 3.26$ light-years.
$d\,(\text{parsecs}) = \dfrac{1}{p\,(\text{arcseconds})}$, and $1$ pc $= 3.26$ ly. A larger parallax means a closer star. Every star's parallax is under $1$ arcsecond.

blocks.html: A star's luminosity is the power it gives off. What we see from Earth is its apparent brightness: the power arriving on each square meter. The two are linked by distance, which parallax can measure.

Picture all the light leaving a star at one instant as a growing bubble. By the time it reaches distance $d$ it is spread evenly over a sphere of area $4\pi d^2$. The total power $L$ has not changed, so each square meter receives $$b = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}.$$ Twice as far, the sphere has $2^2 = 4$ times the area, so the same light is spread four times thinner. This inverse-square law also works backward: measure $b$ and $d$, and you get $L = 4\pi d^2 b$.
Apparent brightness $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$: it falls off as the square of the distance. Twice as far means a quarter as bright.

blocks.html: The same law sets how much sunlight each planet gets. Jupiter, at $5.2$ AU, receives $\frac{1}{5.2^2} = \frac{1}{27}$ of the sunlight Earth does, one reason its icy moons stay frozen. Later, standard candles use this law in reverse to measure distances to galaxies.

A natural guess is that a star twice as far away looks half as bright. But light spreads in all directions, over an area that grows as $d^2$, so the star looks a quarter as bright. Check: Mars is $1.52$ AU from the Sun and gets $\frac{1}{1.52^2} = 0.43$ of the sunlight Earth gets, not $\frac{1}{1.52} = 0.66$.

blocks.html: Astronomers still use a brightness scale invented over 2000 years ago. The Greek astronomer Hipparchus sorted the stars into six classes: the brightest were "first magnitude," the faintest he could see "sixth magnitude." So on this scale, smaller numbers mean brighter stars. It measures apparent brightness in a way that matches how our eyes judge it: by ratios.

Our eyes respond to brightness by ratios, not differences: each step down the old scale looked about equally dimmer, and it turned out each step was the same factor. In 1856 Norman Pogson made this exact: $5$ magnitudes is a factor of exactly $100$. So one magnitude is a factor of $\sqrt[5]{100} = 2.512$, and a difference of $\Delta m$ magnitudes means a brightness ratio of $$\frac{b_1}{b_2} = 100^{\Delta m/5} = 2.512^{\Delta m}.$$ This is an exponential function: adding magnitudes multiplies brightness. Going the other way, $\Delta m = 2.5 \log_{10}\frac{b_1}{b_2}$. The scale extends past zero for very bright objects: Sirius is $-1.46$, Venus up to $-4.6$, the full Moon $-12.7$ and the Sun $-26.7$.
Smaller (and negative) magnitudes are brighter. A difference of $5$ magnitudes is a factor of $100$ in brightness; $1$ magnitude is a factor of $2.512$.

blocks.html: Spread a star's light into a spectrum and you see dark absorption lines. Around 1900, astronomers at Harvard, led by Annie Jump Cannon, sorted hundreds of thousands of stellar spectra by their patterns of lines. The classes they settled on, in order, are O, B, A, F, G, K, M, and they turned out to be a sequence of temperature, from the hottest (O) to the coolest (M).

Most stars are made of nearly the same mix: about three-quarters hydrogen and a quarter helium by mass, with a sprinkle of everything else (as Cecilia Payne showed in 1925). Their spectra differ because temperature decides what state the atoms are in. In cool M stars, molecules such as titanium oxide survive and make broad bands. In K and G stars, metals like calcium and iron show strongly. Hydrogen's visible lines need electrons sitting in level 2; that needs heat, but too much heat strips hydrogen's electron off entirely, so these lines peak in A stars near $10{,}000$ K. Only the hottest O stars can ionize helium, so their spectra show ionized-helium lines. Each class is split into subclasses 0 to 9; the Sun is a G2 star.

blocks.html: Around 1911 to 1913, Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell each plotted stars by two numbers: their spectral class (temperature) and their luminosity. Instead of a random scatter, the stars fell into a few distinct groups. This Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram is the most useful picture in stellar astronomy.

items: Axes: luminosity goes up (on a log scale, from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{6}$ Suns); surface temperature goes along the bottom, increasing to the left, so O stars are on the left and M stars on the right.
Main sequence: a band from hot and bright (upper left) to cool and dim (lower right). About 90% of stars, including the Sun, are here, fusing hydrogen in their cores.
Giants and supergiants: upper right: cool but very luminous.
White dwarfs: lower left: hot but very dim.

blocks.html: Why must cool, luminous stars be huge, and hot, dim ones tiny? Because of luminosity, size and temperature: $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$. A star on the right is cool, so each square meter gives off little light; to be very luminous it must have an enormous surface. A star at the lower left is hot, so each square meter is very bright; to be dim overall it must be very small. Lines of equal radius run diagonally across the diagram: supergiants hundreds of times the Sun's radius, white dwarfs about the size of Earth.

On the H–R diagram, luminosity increases upward and temperature increases to the left. Main-sequence stars lie on a diagonal band; giants sit above it to the right (big), white dwarfs below it to the left (small).

blocks.html: About half of the stars like the Sun have at least one companion star. Pairs bound by gravity, binary stars, are a gift: by weighing with orbits they give the masses of stars, the one property we cannot read from light alone. And when those masses are put on the H–R diagram, they explain the main sequence.

The two stars orbit their common center of mass, the balance point between them. Like children on a seesaw, the heavier star sits closer: $M_1 r_1 = M_2 r_2$. Both go around in the same time, so each one's speed is proportional to its distance from the center: $\frac{M_1}{M_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{v_2}{v_1}$. Newton's form of Kepler's third law gives their total mass from the size $a$ (in AU) and period $P$ (in years) of their orbit: $M_1 + M_2 = \frac{a^3}{P^2}$. With the sum and the ratio, each mass follows. The speeds come from Doppler shifts; the sizes from watching the stars move across the sky, or from eclipses when the orbit is edge-on.

For a binary: $M_1 + M_2 = \dfrac{a^3}{P^2}$ (solar masses, AU, years) and $\dfrac{M_1}{M_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$. Binaries show that the main sequence is a sequence of mass: luminosity rises roughly as $M^{3.5}$.

blocks.html: It is tempting to read the main sequence as a life story, with stars sliding down it as they age. Binary masses show something else: along the main sequence, mass changes. A $10\,M_\odot$ star is thousands of times more luminous than the Sun, and a $0.2\,M_\odot$ red dwarf less than a hundredth as luminous. A star stays near one spot on the main sequence for most of its life. Check: in binaries, the brighter main-sequence star is always the more massive one.

blocks.html: Every star, the Sun included, was born from a cloud of gas and dust. The most likely birthplaces are giant molecular clouds: cold (about 10 to 20 K), dark, and dense by the standards of space, with enough gas for thousands of stars. The Orion Nebula is a nearby nursery, about 1300 light-years away, where new stars are forming today.

Two things fight in a cloud: gravity pulls it in, and the gas pressure of its warm, jostling molecules pushes out. Cold gas pushes weakly, so in a cold, dense clump gravity wins and the clump collapses. As it falls inward it loses gravitational energy, and roughly half of that energy heats the gas while the rest is radiated away (the virial theorem). So a collapsing protostar heats up even as it shines. It keeps shrinking and heating until its core reaches about 10 million K. Then hydrogen begins to fuse, as in how the Sun shines, the core makes as much energy as the star radiates, and the outward pressure balances gravity. A star is born on the main sequence.
Stars form when cold, dense clumps of gas and dust collapse under their own gravity. Contraction heats the protostar until its core reaches about 10 million K and hydrogen fusion begins.

It is the other way around: stars form first, from collapsing gas clouds, and planets form afterward in the disks around them. blocks.html: You estimated the Sun's lifetime as fuel divided by the rate of use. Binary stars showed how luminosity depends on mass. Put the two together, and you can predict how long any main-sequence star will last.

A star's fuel is proportional to its mass $M$ (each burns about the same fraction of its hydrogen on the main sequence). The rate it uses fuel is its luminosity, which grows steeply with mass: roughly $L \propto M^{3.5}$. So the lifetime goes as $$t \propto \frac{M}{L} \propto \frac{M}{M^{3.5}} = M^{-2.5}.$$ Scaling to the Sun's 10 billion years: $t \approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times M^{-2.5}$ (with $M$ in solar masses). A heavier star has more fuel, but its stronger gravity squeezes its core hotter and denser, and fusion speeds up far more than the fuel supply grows.

Main-sequence lifetime $\approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times \dfrac{M}{L} \approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times M^{-2.5}$. Massive stars live fast and die young; small stars last for hundreds of billions of years.

blocks.html: A star spends about 90% of its life on the main sequence. When the hydrogen in its core runs out, as described in main-sequence lifetimes, its life changes fast. For a star like the Sun, here is what happens next.

With no fusion in the core, nothing supplies the heat that held it up, so gravity squeezes the core of helium; squeezing heats it. Hydrogen just outside the core now gets hot enough to fuse in a shell, faster than the core ever did. The extra energy pushes the star's outer layers outward, and the star swells to tens or hundreds of times its old radius. Its surface, spread over a far larger area, cools to about $3500$ to $4500$ K and glows orange-red: a red giant, cooler but far more luminous. When the core reaches about 100 million K, helium nuclei fuse into carbon and oxygen. Once the helium runs out, a Sun-like star cannot squeeze its core hot enough for the next step. Its outer layers drift off as a glowing planetary nebula (nothing to do with planets), and the bare core is left: a white dwarf.

When core hydrogen runs out, a Sun-like star swells into a red giant, later fuses helium into carbon and oxygen, then sheds its outer layers. Its core remains as a white dwarf: about the Sun's mass packed into a ball the size of Earth, slowly cooling.

blocks.html: The Sun will not become a black hole or explode as a supernova; those fates need stars of more than about 8 solar masses. Check the path: red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf, which is just what we see around many stars in our galaxy today.

blocks.html: We cannot watch a star age for billions of years, but we can read ages from star clusters. A cluster is a family of stars born together from one cloud: open clusters such as the Pleiades hold hundreds to thousands of stars, and globular clusters hold hundreds of thousands, packed into a ball. Plotting a cluster on the H–R diagram works like a clock, using what you know about how stars leave the main sequence.

All the stars in a cluster formed at nearly the same time, but with a wide range of masses. Massive stars burn out first. So as a cluster ages, its main sequence is eaten away from the top: the hottest, brightest stars peel off to become giants, then the next ones, and so on. The point where the main sequence ends, the turnoff, marks the stars that are just now running out of core hydrogen. Their main-sequence lifetime equals the cluster's age: $t \approx 10\ \text{billion years} \times M_{\text{turnoff}}^{-2.5}$.
A cluster's age equals the main-sequence lifetime of the stars at its turnoff. The lower the turnoff on the main sequence, the older the cluster.

blocks.html: A star of more than about 8 solar masses does not stop at helium. After it becomes a red giant (a red supergiant), its heavy core can squeeze itself hot enough for one fusion stage after another: carbon, neon, oxygen, then silicon, building up a core of layers like an onion. Each stage is shorter than the last; silicon burns in about a day. Then the core reaches iron, and the star's life ends in seconds.

Fusion releases energy only when the products are more tightly bound than the fuel. Binding energy per nucleon climbs from hydrogen up to a peak at iron and nickel, about $8.8$ MeV, then falls for heavier nuclei. So fusing anything lighter than iron releases energy, but fusing iron would absorb it. With no energy source, the iron core, about as massive as the Sun and as big as Earth, loses its support and collapses in less than a second, to a ball of neutrons about 20 km across. The infalling layers rebound off it, and a huge burst of neutrinos helps drive them outward: a core-collapse supernova, for weeks as bright as billions of Suns.
Massive stars fuse elements up to iron. Iron cannot release energy by fusion, so the core collapses and the star explodes, scattering the elements it made, and new ones made in the blast, into space.

blocks.html: It is easy to assume fusion can go on forever, but a star cannot make energy by fusing iron: iron nuclei are already the most tightly bound, so joining them would take energy in. That is exactly why the core collapses. Check the curve: binding energy per nucleon rises up to iron and falls after it.

Supernovae are how the elements in your body got here. Carbon, oxygen, calcium and iron were made in stars and blown into space by supernovae and stellar winds; many elements heavier than iron, like gold, come from the rapid neutron captures in supernovae and in collisions of neutron stars. A different kind, the type Ia supernova, is a white dwarf in a binary that grows past about 1.4 solar masses and blows itself apart.

blocks.html: A core-collapse supernova leaves something behind. The collapsing iron core is crushed until its electrons are forced into its protons, turning them into neutrons. What remains is a neutron star: more mass than the Sun in a ball about 20 kilometers across, the size of a city.

Two things are conserved as the core shrinks from thousands of kilometers to about 10 km in radius, and both get concentrated. Its angular momentum ($\propto r^2\omega$) stays the same, so as $r$ drops by a factor of hundreds, the spin rate rises by a factor of hundreds of thousands: a core turning once a day ends up spinning several times a second. Its magnetic field is squeezed too, reaching trillions of times the strength of Earth's. Charged particles race along the field lines and beam radiation out from the two magnetic poles. The magnetic axis is usually tilted from the spin axis, so the beams sweep around the sky like a lighthouse's. If one sweeps across Earth, we see a pulse once per rotation: a pulsar.

A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star: about 1.2 to 2 solar masses, about 20 km across, as dense as an atomic nucleus. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.

steps: One cubic centimeter would have a mass of about 670 million tonnes.

blocks.title: The Crab pulsar
blocks.q: The Crab pulsar, the neutron star at the heart of the Crab Nebula, pulses $30$ times a second. What is its spin period, and how fast is its equator moving if its radius is $10$ km?
steps: Equator speed: $\frac{2\pi \times 10{,}000\ \text{m}}{0.033\ \text{s}} = 1.9 \times 10^{6}$ m/s, about $0.6\%$ of the speed of light.

blocks.html: Pulsars do not pulse by swelling and shrinking. Nothing that big could vibrate that fast, but a city-sized ball can spin that fast. The pulses are a beam sweeping past, like a lighthouse seen from a ship. Check: pulsar pulses are as regular as atomic clocks and slow down only very gradually as the star loses spin energy.
Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student, discovered the first pulsar in 1967 as a strange, regular radio signal.

blocks.html: If the core left by a supernova has more than about 3 solar masses, not even the neutron pressure that holds up a neutron star can support it, and nothing known can stop the collapse. The result is a black hole. The idea grows out of escape speed: the more mass squeezed into a smaller ball, the faster you must go to leave its surface.

Escape speed is $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$. Squeeze a mass $M$ small enough and the escape speed reaches the speed of light $c$. Setting $\sqrt{2GM/r} = c$ gives $$R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2},$$ the Schwarzschild radius. Einstein's general relativity gives exactly this radius for the event horizon: nothing that crosses it, not even light, ever comes back out. For the Sun's mass, $R_s$ is about $3$ km; it grows in proportion to mass, about $2.95$ km per solar mass. Far outside the horizon, though, a black hole's gravity is just $\frac{GM}{r^2}$, the same as any star of that mass.
A black hole's event horizon has radius $R_s = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}$, about $3$ km per solar mass. Inside it, nothing escapes. Far away, a black hole pulls exactly like any other object of the same mass.

blocks.cap: A 10-solar-mass black hole drawn to scale: its event horizon is about $30$ km in radius. The dashed circle is the innermost stable orbit, at three times that.

blocks.title: A stellar black hole
blocks.q: Find the event-horizon radius of a black hole of $10$ solar masses ($1.99 \times 10^{31}$ kg).
steps: $R_s = 2.95 \times 10^{4}$ m $\approx 30$ km: ten Suns' worth of mass inside a city-sized sphere.

blocks.title: The giant at our galaxy's center
blocks.q: Sagittarius A* has about $4.3 \times 10^{6}$ solar masses. How big is its event horizon, in AU?
steps: In AU: $\frac{1.27 \times 10^{7}}{1.496 \times 10^{8}} = 0.085$ AU, smaller than Mercury's orbit.
Its mass was found from stars orbiting it, using orbits as scales.

blocks.html: Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners. Outside the horizon, gravity follows the same $GM/r^2$ as always. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep orbiting exactly as it does (in the dark). Only things that come very close, within a few times $R_s$, are in danger. Check: stars orbit Sagittarius A* on stable ellipses, year after year.

Evidence for black holes: X-ray-bright gas swirling into unseen companions of several to about 20 solar masses (such as Cygnus X-1), stars orbiting Sagittarius A*, the gravitational waves from merging black holes first detected by LIGO in 2015, and the Event Horizon Telescope's images of the dark shadows of M87* (2019) and Sagittarius A* (2022).

blocks.html: On a dark night, far from city lights, a faint glowing band arches across the sky. Galileo's telescope showed it is made of countless faint stars. It is our galaxy, the Milky Way, seen from inside. Because light takes time to travel, even its starlight is old: light from the far side of the galaxy set out about 100,000 years ago.

Why a band? The Milky Way is a flat disk, and we live inside it. Look along the disk and your line of sight passes through thousands of light-years of stars, blurring into a glow; look out of the disk and you see far fewer. Dust in the disk dims and hides the distant parts, which is why astronomers long thought the Sun was near the center. In 1918 Harlow Shapley mapped the globular clusters, which swarm around the true center, and found it lies far away in the direction of Sagittarius. Infrared and radio telescopes, which see through dust, have since mapped the whole structure.

items: Disk: about 100,000 light-years across but only about 1000 thick, with spiral arms of gas, dust and young stars. The Sun lies in it, about 26,000 light-years from the center.
Bulge and bar: a thick, crowded central region of mostly older stars, crossed by a bar.
Center: a black hole, Sagittarius A*, of about 4 million solar masses.
Halo: a faint, roughly round cloud of old stars and globular clusters surrounding the disk.

blocks.html: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy of a few hundred billion stars, a disk about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun is in the disk, about 26,000 light-years from the center, orbiting it about once every 220 million years.
