blocks.html: Two old ideas linger: that the Milky Way is the whole universe, and that the Sun sits at its center. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that "spiral nebulae" such as Andromeda are galaxies far outside our own, and the observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies. And the Sun is in the outer disk, about halfway out. Check: the Milky Way's band looks brightest and thickest toward Sagittarius, the direction of the center, not evenly all around.

blocks.html: Beyond the Milky Way lie hundreds of billions of other galaxies. In 1926 Edwin Hubble sorted the ones he could see by shape, and his scheme is still used. Shape turns out to tell a lot about a galaxy's gas, its stars and its history.

items: Elliptical (E0 to E7): smooth, featureless ovals of stars, with little gas or dust. The number gives how flattened the image looks: $n = 10\left(1 - \frac{b}{a}\right)$, from E0 (round) to E7 (most stretched). The largest galaxies of all are giant ellipticals.

Spiral (Sa, Sb, Sc): a bright central bulge in a flat disk with spiral arms, rich in gas and dust. From Sa to Sc the bulge shrinks and the arms open up. Barred spirals (SBa to SBc) have arms that start from the ends of a bar of stars through the center. The Milky Way is a barred spiral.
Irregular: no regular shape, often small and gas-rich, like the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.

blocks.html: A galaxy's colors come from its stars. Hot, massive blue stars live only a few million years, so a galaxy that looks blue must be making new stars, which needs gas. Spiral arms and irregulars are full of gas and glow with young blue stars and pink nebulae. Ellipticals have used up or lost their gas long ago; with no new stars, only long-lived red and yellow stars remain, so they look reddish. Many large ellipticals are thought to have grown through mergers of smaller galaxies, which scrambles orderly disks into rounded swarms.

Galaxies come as ellipticals (smooth, old red stars, little gas), spirals and barred spirals (disks with arms, gas and young blue stars) and irregulars (no clear shape, gas-rich). The Milky Way is a barred spiral.

blocks.html: Pictures of galaxies tend to show beautiful spirals, so many people think every galaxy is a spiral like ours. Ellipticals are common, especially in crowded clusters of galaxies, and small dwarf galaxies, mostly faint ellipticals and irregulars, are the most numerous of all. Check: our own neighborhood, the Local Group, has three big spirals (the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum) and dozens of dwarfs.

blocks.html: You can weigh anything with an orbit. Apply that to the stars and gas circling the center of the Milky Way and other galaxies, and the answer is startling: galaxies have far more mass than all their stars and gas.

For a star on a circular orbit of radius $r$, gravity from the mass $M$ inside the orbit supplies the centripetal force: $\frac{GM}{r^2} = \frac{v^2}{r}$, so $$M = \frac{v^2 r}{G}.$$ Most of a galaxy's light comes from its center. If the light showed where the mass is, then far out, beyond most of the stars, $M$ would stop growing, and speeds would fall off as $v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$, like planets around the Sun. Measured rotation curves, pioneered by Vera Rubin and Kent Ford in the 1970s, show instead that speeds stay about the same, far beyond the visible disk. A flat curve ($v$ constant) means $M \propto r$: the enclosed mass keeps growing with distance, in a huge halo of matter we cannot see: dark matter.

Stars and gas far out in galaxies orbit too fast for the visible mass. Using $M = v^2r/G$, galaxies hold several times more mass than we see. This dark matter makes up about $85\%$ of all matter; what it is remains unknown.

blocks.q: The Sun orbits $26{,}000$ light-years ($2.46 \times 10^{20}$ m) from the galactic center at $220$ km/s. How much mass lies inside its orbit?

blocks.title: What the visible mass predicts
blocks.q: Stars $30{,}000$ light-years out orbit at $220$ km/s. If nearly all the mass were inside that distance, how fast would stars at $120{,}000$ light-years move?
steps: With the same mass inside, $v \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}$: four times as far means half as fast.
Predicted: $110$ km/s. Measured speeds that far out stay near $200$ km/s, so the mass keeps growing: dark matter.
blocks.a: About $110$ km/s, if there were no dark matter.

blocks.html: A reasonable first guess is that dark matter is just ordinary dust, gas, dim stars and planets we have not counted. Those have been searched for: dust glows in infrared, gas in radio and X-rays, and dim stars and black holes would bend the light of stars behind them, which surveys looked for. Above all, the amounts of light elements made in the Big Bang and the pattern in the cosmic microwave background both cap ordinary matter at about one-sixth of all matter. Check: other evidence agrees, from the speeds of galaxies in clusters to gravitational lensing, which maps mass by how it bends light.

What dark matter is made of is an open question. The leading idea is a kind of particle that feels gravity but does not interact with light; experiments are searching for it, so far without a confirmed detection.

blocks.html: Parallax works only for nearby stars. To reach other galaxies, astronomers use standard candles: objects whose luminosity $L$ is known. Measure how bright one looks, $b$, and the inverse-square law gives its distance: $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{4\pi b}}$.

The hard part is knowing $L$. Cepheid variables are pulsating yellow supergiant stars that brighten and dim every few days to a few months. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud (all about the same distance from us), found that the longer a Cepheid's period, the more luminous it is. So timing a Cepheid tells its luminosity, and its brightness then tells its distance. Cepheids are bright enough to see in galaxies tens of millions of light-years away. For greater distances, astronomers use type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs that blow up at nearly the same mass and so peak at nearly the same luminosity, about 5 billion Suns, visible billions of light-years away. Each rung is calibrated by the one below: parallax fixes the nearest Cepheids, Cepheids fix the supernovae.

A standard candle has a known luminosity, so its apparent brightness gives its distance: for two of the same kind, $\dfrac{d_2}{d_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}}$. Cepheids (period tells luminosity) and type Ia supernovae (nearly equal peaks) are the main ones.

blocks.html: In the 1910s Vesto Slipher found that the spectral lines of most galaxies are redshifted: they are moving away from us. In 1929 Edwin Hubble combined those speeds with distances from Cepheids and found a simple pattern (Georges Lemaître had predicted it two years earlier): the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes, in proportion.

The rule is $v = H_0 d$, the Hubble–Lemaître law. $H_0$, the Hubble constant, is measured at about $70$ km/s per megaparsec (recent measurements range from about 67 to 73). Why proportional? Imagine space itself stretching evenly, like a sheet of rubber with dots on it, or raisin bread rising. If every distance grows by $1\%$ in some time, a galaxy $100$ Mpc away moves $1$ Mpc farther while one $200$ Mpc away moves $2$ Mpc: twice the distance, twice the speed. And the same is true seen from any dot. So the law is exactly what uniform expansion of the universe looks like from inside it. (For galaxies far away, the redshift is best understood as light's wavelength stretching along with space.)
Hubble–Lemaître law: $v = H_0 d$, with $H_0 \approx 70$ km/s/Mpc. Galaxies recede faster the farther away they are, because the universe is expanding, everywhere at once.

But in a uniformly expanding universe, every observer sees the same thing: all the other galaxies receding, faster when farther. There is no center. blocks.html: If galaxies are flying apart now, as Hubble's law shows, then in the past they were closer together. Run the expansion backward and everything comes together at one time in the past: the start of the expansion. How long ago?

A galaxy at distance $d$ moving at $v = H_0 d$ would have taken $t = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{d}{H_0 d} = \frac{1}{H_0}$ to get there, if the speed never changed. Notice that $d$ cancels: every galaxy gives the same time. This Hubble time, $1/H_0$, estimates the age of the universe. The units need care: $H_0 = 70$ (km/s)/Mpc is a speed divided by a distance. Writing $1$ Mpc as $3.086 \times 10^{19}$ km makes the kilometers cancel: $H_0 = \frac{70}{3.086 \times 10^{19}}$ per second $= 2.27 \times 10^{-18}$ s⁻¹. Then $\frac{1}{H_0} = 4.41 \times 10^{17}$ s $= 14.0$ billion years. A handy shortcut: $\frac{1}{H_0} \approx \frac{978}{H_0}$ billion years, with $H_0$ in km/s/Mpc.
Age of the universe $\approx \dfrac{1}{H_0}$. With $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc, $1/H_0 \approx 14$ billion years; detailed models give $13.8$ billion years.

blocks.q: If $H_0$ were $73$ km/s/Mpc, what would $1/H_0$ be?
steps: $\frac{978}{73} = 13.4$ billion years: faster expansion means less time to reach today's distances.

blocks.html: The most common slip is with the units of $H_0$. Dividing 1 by 70 gives 0.014, which is not an age in any unit. You must first convert megaparsecs to kilometers so the distance units cancel, leaving 1/seconds. Check the size: the answer should be about 14 billion years, a little older than the oldest stars we know (about 12 to 13 billion years).

$1/H_0$ assumes the expansion rate never changed. In fact gravity slowed it early on and dark energy has sped it up lately; the effects nearly cancel, so the measured age, $13.8$ billion years (from the Planck mission), is close to $1/H_0$.

blocks.html: The age of the universe comes from running the expansion backward. Going back, everything was closer together, denser and hotter, until about 13.8 billion years ago the universe was extremely hot and dense. That is the Big Bang theory: not an explosion at a point, but the expansion and cooling of space from that hot, dense state. Three separate lines of evidence support it.

items: The expansion. Galaxies recede according to Hubble's law, so they were once much closer.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB). A faint glow of microwaves from every direction, a nearly perfect blackbody at $2.725$ K, found by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965. It is light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe had cooled to about 3000 K and atoms could form, letting light travel freely. Expansion has since stretched it a thousandfold into microwaves.

The light elements. In the first few minutes the universe was a nuclear furnace that made helium from hydrogen before it cooled too much. Theory predicts about $75\%$ hydrogen and $25\%$ helium by mass, with traces of deuterium and lithium, which is what we find in the oldest stars and gas.

blocks.html: Stretching space stretches light: a wavelength grows in proportion to the size of the universe, $1 + z = \frac{\text{size now}}{\text{size then}}$. By Wien's law, a longer peak wavelength means a lower temperature, so the radiation's temperature falls as the universe grows: $T = T_{\text{now}}(1 + z)$. The CMB came from redshift about 1100, when the temperature was $2.725 \times 1101 \approx 3000$ K, just when hydrogen atoms could form. A hot, dense past predicts this glow everywhere, with exactly a blackbody's shape, and that is what satellites (COBE, WMAP, Planck) measured.

The Big Bang is the expansion and cooling of the universe from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. Evidence: the expansion, the cosmic microwave background at $2.725$ K, and the amounts of hydrogen and helium.

steps: At that temperature hydrogen nuclei can just hold on to their electrons, so the universe turned transparent.

blocks.html: It is natural to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off at one spot in empty space, with galaxies flying out from there. The evidence says space itself expanded everywhere at once. There is no center, and the CMB arrives evenly from every direction because every part of space was part of the hot early universe. Check: if galaxies flew out from one point, we could find the point; Hubble's law looks the same from every galaxy.

blocks.html: Gravity pulls everything toward everything else, so after the Big Bang the expansion should be slowing down. In the 1990s two teams set out to measure how fast it was slowing, using type Ia supernovae billions of light-years away. In 1998 both found the opposite: the expansion is speeding up.

A type Ia supernova's brightness gives its distance, and its redshift tells how much the universe has expanded since its light left. Comparing the two maps the history of the expansion. The distant supernovae looked fainter than expected in a universe that was slowing down, typically by about 20 to 25%. Fainter means farther ($b \propto 1/d^2$): a supernova at $75\%$ of the expected brightness is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.75}} = 1.15$ times as far. So the universe expanded more than expected since those explosions: the expansion has been accelerating for roughly the last 5 billion years. Something works against gravity on the largest scales. We do not know what it is, so we call it dark energy. The leading idea is an energy of empty space itself (Einstein's cosmological constant). The discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Distant type Ia supernovae show that the universe's expansion is speeding up. The unknown cause, called dark energy, makes up about $68\%$ of the universe's energy; dark matter about $27\%$ and ordinary matter about $5\%$.
